choices.a: The volume measured in the first second of a forced breath out
choices.b: The expiratory reserve volume plus the residual volume
choices.c: The tidal volume plus the residual volume
choices.d: The vital capacity minus the tidal volume

questions.explanation: FRC is the volume left in the lungs at the end of a quiet breath, where lung recoil and chest-wall recoil balance: ERV + RV. Because it includes the residual volume, spirometry alone can't measure it.
questions.learning_objective: Define FRC and explain why spirometry cannot measure it.

questions.prompt: A 62-year-old smoker's spirometry shows FEV1 1.8 L and FVC 3.6 L. What pattern is this?

choices.d: Normal: both values are within range

questions.explanation: FEV1/FVC = 1.8/3.6 = 0.5, well below 0.7: airflow obstruction, as in COPD. Restriction is suggested by low volumes with a normal or high ratio and confirmed by a low TLC.
questions.learning_objective: Interpret FEV1/FVC to identify an obstructive pattern.

questions.prompt: A baby born at 28 weeks develops rapid breathing, grunting and collapsing alveoli within hours of birth. What is missing?

choices.c: Surfactant, made by type II pneumocytes

questions.explanation: Surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension, which would otherwise collapse small alveoli (Laplace: P = 2T/r). Type II pneumocytes make enough of it only late in gestation, so premature infants develop neonatal respiratory distress syndrome; antenatal corticosteroids speed its production.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the role of surfactant and neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

questions.prompt: A patient with a dense lobar pneumonia stays hypoxemic even on 100% oxygen. What is the main mechanism?

choices.a: Shunt: blood passes through alveoli that are filled and not ventilated
choices.b: A left shift of the oxygen–hemoglobin curve
choices.d: Dead space: alveoli ventilated but not perfused

questions.explanation: Consolidated alveoli are perfused but not ventilated (V/Q = 0), so that blood returns deoxygenated and mixes with oxygenated blood. Extra inspired oxygen can't reach it, so shunt hypoxemia responds poorly to supplemental O₂, unlike V/Q mismatch.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize shunt physiology and its poor response to oxygen.

questions.prompt: Which change shifts the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right?

choices.b: A rise in PCO₂ and fall in pH, as in exercising muscle

questions.explanation: Increased CO₂, H⁺ (the Bohr effect), 2,3-BPG and temperature lower hemoglobin's affinity for O₂, shifting the curve right and aiding unloading in tissues. Carbon monoxide, fetal hemoglobin, cold and alkalosis shift it left.
questions.learning_objective: List the factors that shift the oxygen–hemoglobin curve right.

questions.prompt: Breathing room air at sea level, a patient has PaCO₂ 40 mmHg and PaO₂ 60 mmHg. Using PAO₂ ≈ 150 − PaCO₂/0.8, what is the A–a gradient, and what does it suggest?

choices.a: About 40 mmHg: normal for any age
choices.c: About 40 mmHg: elevated, pointing to a problem in the lung (V/Q mismatch, shunt or diffusion)

questions.explanation: PAO₂ ≈ 150 − 40/0.8 = 100 mmHg; A–a gradient = 100 − 60 = 40 mmHg, well above normal (roughly 5–15, higher with age). Pure hypoventilation lowers PaO₂ with a normal gradient.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate and interpret the alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient.

questions.prompt: A patient is hypoxemic only because an opioid overdose has slowed his breathing. What happens to the A–a gradient?

choices.c: It can't be calculated in hypoventilation.
choices.d: It stays normal: alveolar and arterial O₂ fall together.

questions.explanation: Hypoventilation raises PaCO₂, which lowers alveolar O₂; the lungs still transfer oxygen normally, so arterial O₂ falls with it and the gradient is preserved.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish hypoventilation from lung disease with the A–a gradient.
